newsitem.title: USA: Serbia opposition wants U.S. support for democracy.
newsitem.headline: Serbia opposition wants U.S. support for democracy.

text.p: A leader of Serbia's opposition coalition on Friday urged the United States to push now for democratic reforms in the former Yugoslavia, rather than pay for much more costly remedies later.

"It is not just a question of moral support for the democratic process, it is a matter of supporting stability in that entire part of the world," Zoran Djindjic told a forum of the United States Institute of Peace.

"Because we know that people here think in a businesslike manner, we can say it would be much cheaper if you would, as a preventive measure, support democracy than to have to remedy the situation by taking the sort of measures that have proved very expensive," said Djindjic, the mayor of Belgrade and one of three leaders of the opposition group Zajedno.
Djindjic and fellow coalition leaders Vesna Pesic and Vuk Daskovic, all of whom addressed the forum, were scheduled to meet later on Friday with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright.
Albright planned to use the meeting to restate the United States' "very strong support" for democratic change in Serbia, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.

"The United States supports the efforts of the Zajedno coalition and the other democratic forces in Serbia to lead Serbia out of the dead end it currently finds itself in, and to begin the process of developing a modern European country," Burns said.

Burns said that while Washington welcomed the Serbian government's implementation of the November municipal elections, "we are distressed" by lack of implementation of other recommendations by an Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe mission.
These recommendations include media reforms, media freedoms and electoral reforms, Burns said.

The opposition coalition's slate of political candidates won in municipal elections in 14 of 15 of the largest cities in Serbia last November. When the government annulled the election results, the coalition organised daily street protests that attracted worldwide media attention.
Pesic, president of the Civic Alliance of Serbia, said the three months of civil protests were "frankly a miracle."
But she said there was no sign that the Serbian government intended to "go further into democratization ... so this is the main conflict."
Draskovic, president of the Serbian Renewal Movement, said the peace envisioned in the Dayton accords could only be realised "by a democratic Serbia."
